chapter_note.about: The control unit turns each instruction into a timed sequence of control signals. This chapter starts with what those signals do: the fetch micro-operations and the single-bus datapath. It then compares the two ways of generating the signals, hardwired gates and a microprogram stored in a control store. It ends with the numbers: how wide and how large the microcode is, how the micro-program counter picks its next value, and how mutually exclusive signals are encoded. GATE asks about this chapter rarely, mostly as one definition question or one sizing question.
chapter_note.simple: The control unit is the conductor of the processor. For every instruction it sends out the right switch signals, one beat at a time, so that registers load and the ALU adds at the right moments. There are two ways to build it. One uses a fixed pattern of logic gates, which is quick but cannot be changed. The other keeps the beats in a table, like a music roll, which is slower but easy to edit. For the table version you must be able to work out how wide each line is and how long the table is, which is just counting bits with powers of two. In exam words: fetch micro-operations, datapath sequencing, hardwired and microprogrammed control, horizontal and vertical microcode, control-store size, micro-sequencing and field encoding.

cards.title: Fetch and micro-operations
cards.simple: Before a processor can do an instruction it has to fetch it, just like going to the shelf and picking up a recipe card. The program counter holds the number of the next card. The processor first copies that number into a register that talks to memory, then memory hands back the card, which is kept in a holding register, and finally the card is moved to the register where it will be read and obeyed. The counter moves on to the next card at the same time. Each tiny copy step is called a micro-operation and takes one clock tick. In exam words: fetch is MAR ← PC; MBR ← M[MAR] with PC ← PC + 1; IR ← MBR, and the arrow shows the direction and the order of the micro-operations matters.
cards.idea: Every instruction starts with a **fetch**: **MAR ← PC**, then **MBR ← M[MAR]** (with **PC ← PC + 1** in parallel), then **IR ← MBR**. Each register transfer is a **micro-operation**, done in one clock step, and the **order** is forced by the data flow.
cards.definition:
Fetch micro-operations:

1. $MAR\leftarrow PC$
2. $MBR\leftarrow M[MAR]$, and in parallel $PC\leftarrow PC+1$
3. $IR\leftarrow MBR$

- PC = program counter, MAR = memory address register, MBR (or MDR) = memory data register, IR = instruction register.
- $X\leftarrow Y$ means: copy the value of $Y$ into $X$.
cards.intuition_full: Memory is accessed only through two registers: the MAR holds the address going out, and the MBR holds the data coming in or going out. So to read an instruction you must first place the address in the MAR, because the memory reads the address from there. Only then can the data appear in the MBR, and only after that can the IR be loaded. That fixes the order: each step needs the result of the one before. The PC increment does not depend on the read result, so it can happen in the same step as the memory read, as long as the datapath has the hardware for it (a separate incrementer or a spare adder). Because the PC is incremented during the fetch, any instruction that uses PC-relative addressing sees the address of the next instruction. Interrupts and calls are the same pattern with other registers: the PC is saved to memory through MBR and MAR, and then loaded with a new address.

examples.setup: PC = 200 and memory word M[200] holds the instruction ADD R1,R2. Show the three micro-operations of the fetch cycle and the register contents after each.
steps: Start: PC = 200 and M[200] = ADD R1,R2. The fetch takes three micro-operations, one per clock step.
T1: MAR ← PC. The address 200 is copied into the memory address register: MAR = 200.
T2: MBR ← M[MAR] and PC ← PC + 1 together (different registers, so they can run in parallel). MBR = ADD R1,R2 and PC = 201.
T3: IR ← MBR. The instruction register now holds ADD R1,R2.
The control unit now decodes IR. PC = 201 already points to the next instruction, so a branch will overwrite PC, not IR.
examples.answer: Fetch: MAR ← PC; MBR ← M[MAR], PC ← PC + 1; IR ← MBR. After it PC = 201 and IR = ADD R1,R2.

examples.setup: A processor performs these micro-operations in order: MBR ← PC; MAR ← 0010 (hex); M[MAR] ← MBR; PC ← 0100 (hex). What is the sequence doing?
steps: MBR ← PC copies the current program counter (the return address) into the data register.
MAR ← 0010 sets the memory address to a fixed location. M[MAR] ← MBR then stores the old PC at address 0010.
PC ← 0100 loads a new program address.
Saving the return address and loading a new PC is the entry to an interrupt or a call: the old PC is kept, and control goes to the handler at 0100.
examples.answer: It is an interrupt (or call) entry: it saves the PC at 0010 and jumps to 0100.

examples.setup: Why can the PC increment run in the same step as MBR ← M[MAR], but IR ← MBR cannot run in that step?
steps: The PC increment needs only the PC, which is already valid, and a free incrementer, so it can start with the read.
IR ← MBR needs the value in MBR, which only appears at the end of the memory read.
So IR ← MBR must wait for the next step.
examples.answer: PC ← PC + 1 is independent of the read result. IR ← MBR depends on it.

cards.title: Datapath sequencing
cards.simple: Inside the processor all registers share one road, called the bus, and only one value can drive the road at a time. The ALU has two inputs but only one comes from the road. The other comes from a holding register Y that was filled earlier. The ALU result is kept in another holding register, Z, because it cannot go straight back onto the busy road. So even a simple sum needs a little choreography: put the first number into Y, put the second on the road while the ALU adds, save the result in Z, and finally put Z on the road to its destination. Each of these moves takes one clock tick. In exam words: on a single bus, one register drives the bus per step; the ALU takes Y and the bus and writes Z; the order follows data dependence.
cards.idea: On a **single bus**, only one value travels per clock step. The ALU adds the holding register **Y** and the bus, and its result goes to **Z**. A sum needs: first operand into Y, second operand on the bus with the ALU operation into Z, then Z to the destination.
cards.definition:
Control signals per step, written as register transfers:

- $X_{out}$ puts register $X$ on the bus. $X_{in}$ loads $X$ from the bus.
- A sum follows the pattern: first operand to $Y$ ($X_{out},Y_{in}$); second operand on the bus with $Add,\ Z_{in}$; then $Z_{out}$ and the destination's in signal.
- A memory read adds a wait step: the data arrives in MDR at the end of the step after MAR is loaded.
cards.intuition_full: The bus is a shared wire, so two registers cannot drive it in the same step. The ALU needs both operands at the same time, but only one can come from the bus. That is why the first operand waits in Y: it is parked in an earlier step. The second operand arrives on the bus during the step in which the ALU works. The ALU output cannot return to the bus in the same step, because the bus is busy with the second operand, so it lands in Z and is moved on in the next step. The order is therefore fixed by what each step needs. A longer expression just repeats the pattern: after each addition, the partial sum in Z must be moved into Y before the next operand is placed on the bus. Memory adds delay. After MAR is loaded and Read is issued, the data is not in MDR until the end of the next step, so the CPU waits one step.

examples.setup: A single-bus datapath has registers R0, R1, R2, a register Y that feeds the ALU's left input, the bus as the ALU's right input, and an output register Z. R0 = 4, R1 = 10, R2 = 7. One clock step performs one set of non-conflicting transfers. Compute R0 ← R0 + R1 + R2 and count the steps.
steps: Step 1: R0out, Yin. R0 puts 4 on the bus and Y stores it: Y = 4.
Step 2: R1out, Add, Zin. R1 puts 10 on the bus, the ALU adds Y + bus = 4 + 10, and Z stores 14.
Step 3: Zout, Yin. Z puts 14 on the bus and Y stores it. The bus carries only one value per step, so Z cannot also feed the ALU in the same step.
Step 4: R2out, Add, Zin. R2 puts 7 on the bus, the ALU adds 14 + 7, and Z stores 21.
Step 5: Zout, R0in. Z puts 21 on the bus and R0 stores it: R0 = 21.
examples.answer: R0 = 21 after 5 clock steps.

examples.setup: Three steps are given for R3 ← R1 − R2 on the same datapath: (a) Zout, R3in; (b) R2out, Sub, Zin; (c) R1out, Yin. In what order must they run?
steps: The ALU's left input is Y, so R1 must be loaded into Y first: step (c) comes first.
Then R2 goes on the bus and the ALU subtracts: Y − bus = R1 − R2, stored in Z: step (b).
Last, the result moves from Z to R3: step (a).
examples.answer: Order c, b, a. Swapping the operands would compute R2 − R1.

examples.setup: R1 ← M[R2] on the same datapath. MAR is loaded from the bus and the read is started in one step, and the data appears in MDR at the end of the following step. How many steps are needed, and what happens if the wait is forgotten?
steps: Step 1: R2out, MARin, Read. The address goes to MAR and the read starts.
Step 2: wait. The memory is working and MDR is not valid yet.
Step 3: MDRout, R1in. MDR puts the data on the bus and R1 loads it.
examples.answer: 3 steps. If the wait is forgotten, R1 loads stale data from MDR at step 2.

cards.title: Hardwired control
cards.simple: A hardwired control unit is like a music box with the tune built into its pins. The instruction decides which row of pins is active and the step counter says which beat we are at. Where an active row meets an active beat, a pin pushes a lever, and that lever is a control signal telling a register to load or the ALU to add. All of this is done with fixed logic gates, so it is very fast, but changing the tune means rebuilding the box. This suits simple instruction sets with few instructions that all look alike. In exam words: hardwired control generates each signal as a gate-level function of the opcode, the time step and the flags; it is fast but hard to change, and typical of RISC.
cards.idea: In **hardwired control** each control signal is a fixed Boolean function of the **instruction**, the **time step** and the **flags**, built from gates. It is **fast** and **hard to change**. It is typical of RISC.
cards.definition:
Each signal is a sum of products of step lines $T_k$, instruction lines and flags, for example

$$Z_{in}=T_5\cdot(ADD+SUB),\qquad PC_{in}=T_4\cdot BRZ\cdot Z$$

- $T_k$ = 1 only in time step $k$ (a one-hot decoded counter).
- Instruction lines come from decoding the opcode in the IR.
- Flags such as $Z$ make a signal depend on data (conditional branches).
cards.intuition_full: At any instant the control unit knows three things: which instruction it is running, which step it is in, and the flags. The signals needed at that instant are a fixed function of those three. The designer writes one equation per signal, listing all the (instruction, step) pairs in which it must fire, and builds it with AND gates for each pair and an OR gate to collect them. Speed comes from the fact that nothing has to be looked up: the signals appear after a few gate delays. The cost is flexibility. The number of equations and gates grows with the number of instructions and steps, and any change to an instruction means redesigning the logic. This is why hardwired control suits RISC, where there are few instructions of regular shape, and why CISC machines with hundreds of complex instructions use microprogrammed control (card c4).

examples.setup: A hardwired control unit has instruction lines ADD and SUB (from the IR decoder) and step lines T4, T5, T6 (from the step counter). The signal equations are: R2out = T4·(ADD+SUB), Yin = T4·(ADD+SUB), R1out = T5·(ADD+SUB), Add = T5·ADD, Sub = T5·SUB, Zin = T5·(ADD+SUB). The IR holds ADD and the counter is at T5. Which signals are asserted?
steps: A hardwired control unit has two kinds of inputs: the decoded instruction (lines ADD, SUB) and the step counter lines (T4, T5, T6). Fixed AND-OR gates combine them into control signals.
The IR holds ADD, so the ADD line is 1 and the SUB line is 0.
The step counter is at T5, so T5 = 1 and T4 = T6 = 0.
Evaluate each equation: R2out = 0·1 = 0 and Yin = 0 (they need T4). R1out = 1·(1+0) = 1. Add = 1·1 = 1. Sub = 1·0 = 0. Zin = 1·(1+0) = 1.
Active signals now: R1out, Add and Zin. R2out, Yin and Sub stay 0. At the next clock the counter moves to T6 and a new set of signals fires.
examples.answer: R1out, Add and Zin are asserted; the others are 0.

examples.setup: A hardwired CPU has 8 instructions and at most 6 time steps per instruction. How many instruction lines and step lines does the control logic need, and how many AND terms can one control signal need at most?
steps: 8 instructions need a 3-to-8 decoder on the opcode: 8 instruction lines.
6 steps need ⌈log₂ 6⌉ = 3 counter bits, decoded into step lines T1 to T6 (6 lines used).
A signal can fire in any (instruction, step) pair: at most 8 × 6 = 48 AND terms.
examples.answer: 8 instruction lines, 6 step lines, and at most 48 AND terms per signal.

examples.setup: The branch-if-zero signal is PCin = T4·BRZ·Z. What is PCin at step T4 of a BRZ instruction when the flag Z is 0 and when Z is 1?
steps: Z = 0: PCin = 1·1·0 = 0. The branch is not taken and PC is not loaded.
Z = 1: PCin = 1·1·1 = 1. The branch is taken and PC is loaded with the target.
A flag in the equation makes the control signal depend on data.
examples.answer: Z = 0 gives PCin = 0, Z = 1 gives PCin = 1. Hardwired logic can use flags directly.

1. A hardwired control unit has two kinds of inputs: the decoded instruction (lines ADD, SUB) and the step counter lines (T4, T5, T6). Fixed AND-OR gates combine them into control signals.
2. The IR holds ADD, so the ADD line is 1 and the SUB line is 0.
3. The step counter is at T5, so T5 = 1 and T4 = T6 = 0.
4. Evaluate each equation: R2out = 0·1 = 0 and Yin = 0 (they need T4). R1out = 1·(1+0) = 1. Add = 1·1 = 1. Sub = 1·0 = 0. Zin = 1·(1+0) = 1.
5. Active signals now: R1out, Add and Zin. R2out, Yin and Sub stay 0. At the next clock the counter moves to T6 and a new set of signals fires.

cards.title: Microprogrammed control
cards.simple: A microprogrammed control unit is like a player piano with a paper roll. The roll holds the tune as a long list of simple instructions, and a pointer walks down it one line at a time. Each line says which control signals to switch on for one clock tick. Every machine instruction has its own short piece of roll, called a microroutine. To find where a piece starts, a small lookup table is consulted. Changing or adding an instruction only means changing the roll, not rebuilding the machine. The price is speed, because every step must read a line from the roll first. In exam words: a control store holds microinstructions; each machine instruction has a microroutine located through a mapping ROM; microprogramming is flexible but slower and typical of CISC.

- **Microroutine:** the sequence of microinstructions for one machine instruction.
- **Mapping ROM:** opcode → start address of the microroutine.
- **μPC:** address of the next microinstruction (it is not the PC of the machine program).
- Every step costs one read of the control store.
cards.intuition_full: Hardwired control spends gates to produce signals directly. Microprogramming spends memory instead. The signals for every instruction and every step are written into a table, and the control unit simply reads the table row by row. The row's bits connect straight to the control lines of the datapath. Everything specific to the instruction set lives in the contents of the table. That makes the design regular and easy to correct or extend: a bug fix is a new table, and a new instruction is a new microroutine plus one entry in the mapping ROM. The same flexibility lets a CISC machine implement complex instructions as a loop of microinstructions. The disadvantage is speed. Each clock step needs a read of the control store before the signals can be applied. A fast control store (ROM or a small RAM) is therefore essential, and a simple RISC pipeline avoids this layer entirely.

cards.title: Horizontal versus vertical microinstructions
cards.simple: Think of a control panel with one switch for every light in a building. That is a horizontal microinstruction: lots of switches, but you can flip any set of them at the same moment, and no extra wiring is needed. A vertical microinstruction is like a keypad: for each group of lights that can never be on together, you type the number of the one you want, and a small decoder lights it. You need far fewer wires, but a decoder per group, and you can only pick one light per group per tick. In exam words: horizontal microinstructions have one bit per control signal (wide, parallel, no decoding); vertical microinstructions encode mutually exclusive signals into fields (narrow, need decoders, less parallelism).
cards.idea: **Horizontal:** one bit per control signal. It is wide and fast, and many signals can fire together. **Vertical:** mutually exclusive signals share an **encoded field**. It is narrow but needs decoders, and one signal per field per step.
cards.definition:
- Horizontal word width = number of control signals.
- Vertical field for $k$ mutually exclusive signals (plus 'none'): $\lceil\log_2(k+1)\rceil$ bits.
- Vertical word width = sum of field widths (independent signals keep one bit each).
- Only mutually exclusive signals may share a field.
cards.intuition_full: Both formats carry the same information. They differ in how much of the decoding is done by the designer and how much by hardware. In a horizontal word, every signal has its own bit, so the datapath receives signals directly. Many signals can be on in one step, so the machine can do things in parallel, but the control store is wide and expensive. In a vertical word, a few bits name which signal in a group is active. A decoder turns that number into the individual signal, which costs gates and a little time. Only signals that can never be on together may share a field, for example the many registers that could put data on a bus, since only one can drive it at once. Independent signals, such as two that can fire together, cannot share a field without losing the ability to fire them in the same step.

examples.setup: A control unit has three groups of mutually exclusive signals: 5 source signals (R0out, R1out, R2out, R3out, PCout), 4 ALU signals (Add, Sub, And, Or) and 3 destination signals (R0in, R1in, Zin). steps: The wanted microinstruction asserts R1out (source), Add (ALU) and Zin (destination). The groups have 5, 4 and 3 signals.
Horizontal: one bit per signal, so 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 bits. Set the bit of R1out, Add and Zin: 01000 1000 001.

Vertical: the signals of one group are mutually exclusive, so each group becomes a field that holds the number of the active signal (0 means none). Field widths: ⌈log₂(5+1)⌉ = 3, ⌈log₂(4+1)⌉ = 3, ⌈log₂(3+1)⌉ = 2 bits.
Fill the fields: R1out is source number 2 = 010, Add is ALU number 1 = 001, Zin is destination number 3 = 11. The vertical word is 010 001 11.
The vertical word has 8 bits against 12. The price: each field needs a decoder, and only one signal per group can be active in a step.
examples.answer: Horizontal: 01000 1000 001 (12 bits). Vertical: 010 001 11 (8 bits).

examples.setup: Three groups of mutually exclusive signals have 6, 11 and 30 signals. Compare the horizontal width with the vertical width.

Vertical total: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 bits.
Saving: 47 − 12 = 35 bits per microinstruction.
examples.answer: 47 bits horizontal, 12 bits vertical, 35 bits saved.

examples.setup: Two independent signals, Zin and Read, can be on in the same step. A designer puts them in one vertical field with a 'none' code. How many bits does the field use, and what is lost?

cards.title: Control word and store size
cards.simple: Each line of the control store is a microinstruction made of three parts. One part holds the actual control signals. One part says which condition to test, if any. One part says where to go next. To work out the size of the whole store you need two things: how wide a line is, and how many lines there are. The number of lines fixes how many bits the 'where next' part needs, because it must be able to name every line. The condition part must be able to name every condition, plus one more choice for 'always'. Then size is lines times width. In exam words: width = control field + condition select + next address; the next-address field is log₂ of the number of words; store size = words × width.
cards.idea: A **microinstruction** = control field + condition-select field + next-address field. The next-address field has **log₂(words)** bits, the select field has **⌈log₂(conditions + 1)⌉** bits, and the control store holds **words × width** bits.
cards.definition:
$$\text{width}=C+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil+\log_2 N,\qquad \text{size}=N\times\text{width}$$

- $C$ = control bits, $m$ = number of conditions (the +1 is the 'always' choice).
- $N$ = number of control store words (a power of two).
- Mapping ROM: one word per opcode value, each word holds a control-store address.
cards.intuition_full: The next-address field must be able to point at any word of the store, so its width is the log of the number of words. If the store has 1024 words, 10 bits are needed. The condition-select field drives a multiplexer that picks which flag decides the branch, so it must name each condition. An unconditional jump or a plain 'go on to the next word' needs its own code, which is why one extra choice, 'always', is added to the count of conditions. Sometimes a question gives the total width and asks you to work backwards: subtract the control bits and the select bits from the width to get the next-address bits, and take 2 to that power for the number of words. The total store size then follows by multiplication. Convert bits to bytes by dividing by 8, and to KiB by dividing by 1024.

examples.setup: A control store has 1024 words. Each microinstruction has 24 control bits, a condition-select field that picks one of 6 conditions or 'always', and a next-address field. Find the width of a microinstruction and the size of the control store.

The condition MUX picks one of 6 conditions or 'always': 7 choices. ⌈log₂ 7⌉ = 3 bits.
Width = 24 + 3 + 10 = 37 bits per microinstruction.
Control store size = 1024 words × 37 bits = 37,888 bits.

examples.setup: A microinstruction is 30 bits wide: 14 bits of micro-operations, X bits of next address and Y bits of MUX select. The MUX picks one of 12 status bits. Find X, Y and the number of words in the control memory.

Ignoring 'always' would give 4 bits for 16 conditions, which is one too few.
examples.answer: 5 select bits for 16 conditions plus 'always', and 4 bits for 15 plus 'always'.

cards.title: Micro-sequencing
cards.simple: The micro-program counter is like a finger on the control store. Most of the time the finger just moves down one line. Sometimes the current line says: if this condition is true, jump to line 23 instead. At the start of a new instruction the finger jumps to wherever the lookup table says the instruction's microroutine begins. At the end of the instruction it jumps back to the fetch routine. So the finger can get its next position from three places: plus one, the jump address on the current line, or the lookup table. A small switch chooses which one to use. In exam words: the μPC takes its next value from μPC + 1, the next-address field or the mapping ROM; a condition-select MUX of ⌈log₂ (conditions+1)⌉ bits picks the flag that decides a branch.
cards.idea: The **μPC** gets its next value from **μPC + 1**, the **next-address field** (a jump) or the **mapping ROM** (start of a new instruction). A **condition-select MUX** picks the flag that decides whether the jump is taken.
cards.definition:
Next μPC =

- $\mu PC+1$ if the condition is false (or no jump),
- next-address field if the selected condition is true,
- mapping ROM output at the start of an instruction.

Mapping ROM size = $2^{\text{opcode bits}}$ words × control-store address bits.
cards.intuition_full: Straight-line microcode needs only an incrementer. Real instructions need three more things. A conditional instruction needs to choose between continuing and jumping, so each microinstruction carries a condition select and a jump address, and a multiplexer picks one flag to test. Decoding a new instruction needs an entry into the right microroutine, so the opcode is looked up in a mapping ROM that holds one start address per opcode value. And the end of a routine has to return to the fetch routine, which is just an unconditional jump to address 0. Putting these together, the sequencing hardware is a multiplexer with three inputs in front of the μPC. This makes the μPC quite different from the ordinary PC, which holds an address in main memory. One machine instruction moves the PC once but the μPC many times.

examples.setup: A micro-sequencer picks the next μPC from three sources: μPC + 1, the next-address field of the current word, and the mapping ROM. A branch-if-zero instruction BRZ has its microroutine at address 20. The microinstruction at 20 has condition select = Z and next-address field = 23. Follow what happens for Z = 0 and for Z = 1.

cards.title: Field encoding
cards.simple: Suppose you want to store which one of 12 buttons is pressed, or that none is pressed. That is 13 different answers. With n bits you can write 2ⁿ different patterns. 3 bits give 8 patterns, which is not enough. 4 bits give 16, which is enough, with a few left over. So the field is 4 bits wide. The extra 'none' answer is the trap: many people forget it and count 12 instead of 13, which can make the answer one bit too small. In exam words: a field that encodes k mutually exclusive signals and a 'none' code needs ⌈log₂(k + 1)⌉ bits.
cards.idea: A field encoding **k mutually exclusive signals** also needs a code for **none**, so it must hold k + 1 values: **⌈log₂(k + 1)⌉ bits**. Only signals that can never be on together may share a field.
cards.definition:
$$b=\lceil\log_2(k+1)\rceil\iff 2^{b-1}<k+1\le 2^b$$

- $k$ = number of mutually exclusive signals in the field.
- The code $0$ means no signal; codes $1\dots k$ select a signal.
- Total bits of a vertical word = sum of $b$ over all fields, plus one bit for each independent signal.
cards.intuition_full: A field is a number. If it must be able to say 'signal 1', 'signal 2' up to 'signal k', that is k different values, and if the step sometimes needs no signal from this group, there is one more value. Counting k + 1 values, the width is the smallest b with 2ᵇ ≥ k + 1. The case k = 7 gives exactly 8 values and 3 bits with nothing wasted. The case k = 8 needs 9 values, so 4 bits, and the extra bit is the price of the 'none' code. Without 'none', 8 signals would fit in 3 bits, but then every step would have to fire one of them, which is rarely true. Groups of signals that can fire together cannot share a field at all. For these the horizontal bit per signal is the right choice. This is the calculation behind the comparison of vertical and horizontal widths in card c5.

examples.setup: One field of a vertical microinstruction must select at most one of 12 mutually exclusive control signals, or none of them. How many bits does the field need, and how does that compare with a horizontal design?
steps: 12 signals plus 'none' make 13 different values to store.
3 bits give 2³ = 8 codes (0 to 7). That is fewer than 13, so 3 bits are not enough.
4 bits give 2⁴ = 16 codes (0 to 15). That is enough, since 13 ≤ 16.
Assign the codes: 0 = none, 1 to 12 = the twelve signals. Codes 13, 14 and 15 are unused.
The encoded field uses 4 bits against 12 for a horizontal design, saving 8 bits per microinstruction.
examples.answer: 4 bits. The rule is ⌈log₂(k + 1)⌉ with k = 12.

examples.setup: Three fields encode groups of 7, 15 and 16 mutually exclusive signals, each with a 'none' code. Find the three field widths, the vertical width and the horizontal width.
steps: 7 signals + none = 8 values: ⌈log₂ 8⌉ = 3 bits (exact fit).
15 signals + none = 16 values: ⌈log₂ 16⌉ = 4 bits (exact fit).
16 signals + none = 17 values: ⌈log₂ 17⌉ = 5 bits. This is one more than 4: the 'none' code pushes it over.
Vertical total: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 bits. Horizontal: 7 + 15 + 16 = 38 bits. Saving: 26 bits.
examples.answer: Widths 3, 4, 5. Vertical 12 bits against horizontal 38 bits.

examples.setup: Two independent signals (they can be on together) are encoded in one field with a 'none' code, instead of two single bits. How many bits does each design use, and which design is more flexible?
steps: Encoded field: Zin, Read and none are 3 values, so ⌈log₂ 3⌉ = 2 bits.
Two separate bits: 2 bits as well. There is no saving.
The field cannot name Zin and Read together, so the two single bits are more flexible.
examples.answer: Both use 2 bits. The separate bits can fire together; the shared field cannot.

cards.why: This one-line formula turns up in every vertical-microcode sizing question. In GATE: find the number of bits in an encoded field or in a whole vertical microinstruction.
how: Count the mutually exclusive signals k in the field.
Add one for the 'none' code: k + 1 values.
Width = smallest b with 2^b ≥ k + 1.
Add up all fields (and one bit per independent signal).
cards.mistake: Forgetting the 'none' code when sizing an encoded field. With k = 15 you still need 4 bits (16 values), but with k = 16 you need 5, not 4.
edge_cases: k = 2^b − 1 fits exactly in b bits with 'none'.
k = 2^b needs b + 1 bits once 'none' is counted.
A field that must always select one signal (no 'none') needs ⌈log₂ k⌉ bits.
The decoder at the output of each field turns b bits back into k+1 lines.
connections: Horizontal versus vertical (card c5) sums these widths over all groups.
Control word and store size (card c6) uses the total width to size the store.

steps.caption: Start: PC = 200 and M[200] = ADD R1,R2. The fetch takes three micro-operations, one per clock step.
T1: MAR ← PC. The address 200 is copied into the memory address register: MAR = 200.
T2: MBR ← M[MAR] and PC ← PC + 1 together (different registers, so they can run in parallel). MBR = ADD R1,R2 and PC = 201.
T3: IR ← MBR. The instruction register now holds ADD R1,R2.
The control unit now decodes IR. PC = 201 already points to the next instruction, so a branch will overwrite PC, not IR.

scenes.title: R0 + R1 + R2 on a single bus in five steps

steps.caption: Step 1: R0out, Yin. R0 puts 4 on the bus and Y stores it: Y = 4.
Step 2: R1out, Add, Zin. R1 puts 10 on the bus, the ALU adds Y + bus = 4 + 10, and Z stores 14.
Step 3: Zout, Yin. Z puts 14 on the bus and Y stores it. The bus carries only one value per step, so Z cannot also feed the ALU in the same step.
Step 4: R2out, Add, Zin. R2 puts 7 on the bus, the ALU adds 14 + 7, and Z stores 21.
Step 5: Zout, R0in. Z puts 21 on the bus and R0 stores it: R0 = 21.

scenes.title: Hardwired signals: instruction line x step line

objects.text:
R1out = T5·(ADD+SUB)   Add = T5·ADD
Zin = T5·(ADD+SUB)   R2out = T4·(ADD+SUB)

steps.caption: A hardwired control unit has two kinds of inputs: the decoded instruction (lines ADD, SUB) and the step counter lines (T4, T5, T6). Fixed AND-OR gates combine them into control signals.
The IR holds ADD, so the ADD line is 1 and the SUB line is 0.
The step counter is at T5, so T5 = 1 and T4 = T6 = 0.
Evaluate each equation: R2out = 0·1 = 0 and Yin = 0 (they need T4). R1out = 1·(1+0) = 1. Add = 1·1 = 1. Sub = 1·0 = 0. Zin = 1·(1+0) = 1.
Active signals now: R1out, Add and Zin. R2out, Yin and Sub stay 0. At the next clock the counter moves to T6 and a new set of signals fires.

scenes.title: A microroutine for ADD read from the control store

steps.caption: The opcode ADD = 1 goes to the mapping ROM, which returns the start address 40. The micro-program counter μPC is loaded with 40.
μPC = 40: the control store word at address 40 asserts R2out and Yin. Then μPC increments.
μPC = 41: the word asserts R1out, Add and Zin.
μPC = 42: the word asserts Zout and R1in. This word is marked END.
END: the μPC is loaded with 0, the start of the fetch microroutine, so the next instruction begins.

scenes.title: The same microinstruction, horizontal and vertical

steps.caption: The wanted microinstruction asserts R1out (source), Add (ALU) and Zin (destination). The groups have 5, 4 and 3 signals.
Horizontal: one bit per signal, so 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 bits. Set the bit of R1out, Add and Zin: 01000 1000 001.

Vertical: the signals of one group are mutually exclusive, so each group becomes a field that holds the number of the active signal (0 means none). Field widths: ⌈log₂(5+1)⌉ = 3, ⌈log₂(4+1)⌉ = 3, ⌈log₂(3+1)⌉ = 2 bits.
Fill the fields: R1out is source number 2 = 010, Add is ALU number 1 = 001, Zin is destination number 3 = 11. The vertical word is 010 001 11.
The vertical word has 8 bits against 12. The price: each field needs a decoder, and only one signal per group can be active in a step.

scenes.title: Width of a microinstruction and the size of the store

steps.caption: 1024 words need ⌈log₂ 1024⌉ = 10 address bits, so the next-address field has 10 bits.
The condition MUX picks one of 6 conditions or 'always': 7 choices. ⌈log₂ 7⌉ = 3 bits.
Width = 24 + 3 + 10 = 37 bits per microinstruction.
Control store size = 1024 words × 37 bits = 37,888 bits.
